title: Strangers and refugees
hookLine: welcoming the newcomer as the Gurus did
tomorrow: the neighbor across the hall knocks too, with bread. who is she?

lines: A DOOR WITH NO NAME YET.
cards: Third floor, end of the hall, a door with no name on it yet. Simran is holding a steel dabba of dal still warm through the lid; her dad, Harjit, has a bag of rotis and a box of mangoes. Arjan opens the door.
Behind him, boxes, a folding table, his little sister on the floor with a coloring book. His family left home because it stopped being safe to stay, and they've been here a few months.
His mom comes to the door, sees the food, and her face closes. Thank you, she says, but we're managing. We don't need charity.
Simran's arms are still full. Now what?

teach.h: WE WERE NEW HERE ONCE TOO.
teach.b: Harjit does something Simran doesn't expect. He says: we were new here once too. And then he asks Arjan's mom how she makes her achar, because Bebe has been complaining about the store kind for years.
The face opens. She tells him, and promises a jar. Here's what he understood.
A welcome isn't a delivery. It's making the newcomer one of us, someone who gives as well as gets.
Guru Arjan says it on Ang 1299, in paraphrase: no one is my enemy, no one is a stranger; I get along with everyone. Notice: not a stranger I'm being kind to. No stranger at all.
And the Gurus' own houses were built that way. In the langar nobody is asked where they're from, what they believe, or whether they can pay; they're handed a plate and a place in the row.

Sikh tradition remembers Guru Nanak himself as a traveler, arriving in towns where he was the stranger at the door. That's the detail to tell a friend tonight: the first Guru of the Sikhs was often the newcomer.
So when the Gurus say welcome, they're speaking from the outside of the door, too. Arjan's mom takes the dal. Then she sets out four cups and says: sit.

how: Gurdwaras serve langar to anyone who comes, without asking who they are, and some Sikh groups help newly arrived families with food, rides and settling in.

o: welcoming the newcomer until there's no stranger left
people who visit a country for a short holiday
a gurdwara service held only for travelers

games.q: the welcome, piece by piece — tap the pairs.
p: a plate and a place, no questions
a traveler, the stranger at the door

s: welcoming a newcomer mostly means giving them things
a welcome makes them one of us, someone who gives as well as gets; Harjit asked for her recipe.
Guru Arjan wrote: no one is my enemy, no one is a stranger
Ang 1299, in paraphrase: I get along with everyone.
the langar asks guests what they believe before serving them
nobody is asked where they're from, what they believe, or whether they can pay.

games.q: a new coworker from overseas eats lunch alone every day and politely says no when you offer to buy her coffee. going by today, what fits best?
o: ask her to recommend a dish from home, and eat lunch with her.
keep buying coffee anyway until she finally says yes.
give her space; she clearly wants to keep to herself.
games.why: Harjit's move: a welcome isn't a delivery. asking for her recipe made her a giver, and no longer a stranger.

practice: Bring to mind someone new in your life: a coworker, a neighbor, a kid in class, a family at your place of worship.
Write them a short message that asks them something, a recipe, a recommendation, their story, instead of only offering. Send it now, or keep it ready for the right moment.

wordCard.voice: Strangers and refugees. Welcoming the newcomer as the Gurus did: no stranger at all, someone who gives as well as gets.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: bigaana, a stranger. Guru Arjan: no one is bigaana (Ang 1299).

carryVoice: Hold this close: welcome the stranger, until there's no stranger left. Four cups on a folding table, and day 1730.

sources.ref: Ang 1299, Raag Kanra, Guru Arjan ('na ko bairee nahee bigaanaa, sagal sang ham kau ban aaee'), paraphrased
